extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, PTAB parties, and appellate litigators (Federal Circuit)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and legal criteria applied by the Federal Circuit in reviewing PTAB final written decisions in IPR appeals concerning obviousness, motions to amend, and related APA/procedural challenges. Intended to guide how courts and the Board evaluate obviousness, optimization arguments, motions to amend, and Director Review procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness legal standard
rubrics_metrics.description: “An obviousness determination requires finding that a person of ordinary skill in the art would have been motivated to combine or modify the teachings in the prior art and would have had a reasonable expectation of success in doing so.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obviousness is reviewed as a question of law de novo, while the Board’s underlying findings of fact (e.g., motivation to combine; reasonable expectation of success) are reviewed for substantial evidence. (Citations: OSI Pharms., Regents of Univ. of Cal. v. Broad Inst., Liqwd v. L’Oreal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantial evidence standard for factual findings
rubrics_metrics.description: “A finding is supported by substantial evidence if a reasonable mind might accept the evidence as adequate to support the finding.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the standard for appellate review of the Board’s factual findings (Consol. Edison). The court will not reweigh evidence or substitute its judgment if the record contains adequate supporting evidence. (Cited repeatedly in the opinion.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Routine optimization / result-effective variable doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: The determination whether a claimed parameter is a result-effective variable is part of a broader routine optimization analysis: 'where the general conditions of a claim are disclosed in the prior art, it is not inventive to discover the optimum or workable ranges by routine experimentation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if a prior-art reference does not disclose a specific parameter for the claimed subject matter, the Board may consider whether that parameter would have been recognized as result-effective; if so, optimization of that parameter is normally obvious. (Citations: In re Aller, In re Antonie, E.I. DuPont, Applied Materials.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Overlap-of-ranges presumption and rebuttal
rubrics_metrics.description: An overlap between a claimed numerical range and a prior-art range creates a presumption of obviousness that can be rebutted with evidence that the parameter was not recognized as result-effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The presumption arises when ranges overlap (Genentech, Applied Materials); but the court explains that the result-effective inquiry is not limited to cases of range overlap—it can be considered when a parameter is not expressly disclosed in the prior art as part of routine optimization analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation-of-success standard (reasonable, not absolute)
rubrics_metrics.description: An expectation of success for obviousness 'need only be reasonable, not absolute.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unpredictability in the art does not preclude obviousness if there was a reasonable probability of success; prior art showing some successes for components can support a reasonable expectation for combined claims. (Citations: Pfizer v. Apotex, Univ. of Strathclyde discussion.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior-art references not limited to working examples
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior art reference is not limited to its specific working examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Board may rely on the general teachings of a reference even when the reference does not exemplify every claimed embodiment; courts will accept that the disclosure of a composition as 'immunogenic' implies immunogenicity rather than requiring explicit experimental exemplars for every serotype. (Cites In re Mills; applied in analysis of GSK-711 and Merck-086.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivation-to-combine and reasonable-expectation-of-success are factual questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a person of ordinary skill would have been motivated to combine references, and whether she would have had a reasonable expectation of success, are questions of fact reviewed for substantial evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence such as overlapping data for related serotypes, routine methods disclosed in the art, expert testimony, and prior demonstrations of immunogenicity can support findings on these factual questions; appellate court will affirm if substantial evidence supports the Board's factual conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of expert testimony and record evidence on appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: The appellate court will not reweigh conflicting expert testimony or other record evidence; it defers to the Board so long as substantial evidence supports the Board’s findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments asking the court to reweigh evidence (e.g., to find unpredictability dispositive) are inappropriate absent lack of substantial evidence. The court emphasizes deference to the Board’s factfinding where the record contains support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motions to amend under §316(d) and 37 C.F.R. §42.121 — patentability inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent owner’s motion to amend (proposing substitute claims) may be denied if the proposed claims are not independently patentable (e.g., are unpatentable as obvious over the prior art).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board must assess whether proposed substitute claims would have been patentable, including analyzing every recited limitation (for example, functional/result limitations like a claimed '2-log increase' in IgG). Denial is reviewed under the APA for arbitrary and capricious agency action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency explanation requirement for motions to amend (reasoned basis enabling review)
rubrics_metrics.description: When denying a motion to amend, the Board must provide a 'reasoned basis' sufficient to enable meaningful judicial review and to prevent the court from supplying reasons the agency did not give.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board must set forth a sufficiently detailed explanation on issues made material by governing law; conclusory statements without analysis of claimed limitations (e.g., ignoring a recited 2‑log IgG result limitation) fail to meet this requirement and warrant remand.

rubrics_metrics.name: APA standard for review of Board's discretionary actions
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board’s denial of a motion to amend is reviewed under the Administrative Procedure Act and must be set aside if 'arbitrary, capricious, an abuse of discretion, or otherwise not in accordance with law.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court will uphold agency decisions of less-than-ideal clarity if the agency’s path can reasonably be discerned, but will not invent rationales not given by the Board (Bowman Transp., SEC v. Chenery).

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmless-error / prejudice requirement for procedural APA challenges
rubrics_metrics.description: If the PTO has procedurally erred (e.g., in how it published Director Review guidance), reversal requires a showing of prejudice; absent prejudice, the error is harmless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The challenger bears the burden to demonstrate prejudicial error; mere changes or lack of notice in PTO guidance do not overturn Board decisions unless the challenger shows it was prejudiced (see Carucel Investors discussion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to analyze all claim limitations including result-limiting functional language
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board must consider whether the incorporation of claimed elements would satisfy not only compositional elements but also any recited functional/result limitations (e.g., immunogenicity metrics such as 'more than a 2-log increase above baseline in serum IgG').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A decision that ignores that a proposed claim requires a specified quantitative result (and fails to analyze whether the prior art would have rendered that result reasonably expected across the recited serotypes) is unsupported by substantial evidence and warrants remand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remand / vacatur when Board fails to support determination with substantial evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: If the Board’s determination that proposed claims are unpatentable is not supported by substantial evidence (or the Board fails to address material claim limitations), the appellate court will vacate and remand for further consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remand is appropriate where Board decisions are silent or conclusory on critical points (e.g., Sanofi Decision’s silence on why proposed claims 48 and 49 would have been obvious given their 2‑log requirement).
